how_to_read: 1. Read the head first: the first 34 lines hold manifest, essence and routing (Read limit=34, or jq '{manifest, essence, routing}' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json).
2. Pick the route for your job and run its jq: jq '<routing[i].jq>' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json
3. Also pull the anti-keywords and review prompts (checks) for your scope: jq '.anti_keywords, .checks' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json

5. Grep works too: every entry is one line, so grep -n '<word>' sticky-punchy-curves.metadump.json returns whole entries.

essence.one_sentence: Punchy is the start and sticky is the stop: one cubic-bezier can carry both as one option, leaving fast, passing its target at most once by a few percent, and settling early into a held rest.
essence.summary: Fast departure, a small overshoot range, early settle and hold; three proposed curves measured against a strict 1 percent band and a loose 5 percent band, presented as loops.

llm_brief.text: Core: three custom cubic-bezier curves, each read as sticky and punchy and each shown as a loop. Punchy is the start: the first window covers most of the distance quickly. Sticky is the stop: the curve is within a settle band of rest early, then holds. One option is a single curve that carries both; another is to split the pair across the set. Two settle bands are offered as options: strict, within 1 percent of rest by about 0.65 of the run; loose, within 5 percent by about 0.35 of the run. Overshoot ranges are proposed, not a rule: 0 to 2 percent is small, 2 to 5 percent is a kick that needs the loose band, above 5 percent reads as a bounce. x1 and x2 stay between 0 and 1; y1 and y2 set the overshoot. Small UI durations sit near 200 to 300 ms, with leaving shorter than entering. The hold lives in the loop, not in the curve: about 0.4 to 0.5 s at each end of a ping-pong, or 1 to 1.5 s between reset-and-hold cycles. Options (proposed, measured): cur-punchy-leave, cubic-bezier(0.2, 1.2, 0.2, 1), 250 ms, about 1.25 percent overshoot, within 1 percent by 0.64 of the run; cur-punchy-sticky, cubic-bezier(0.15, 1, 0.2, 1.04), 300 ms, about 1 percent overshoot, within 1 percent by 0.46; cur-sticky-settle, cubic-bezier(0.18, 0.98, 0.3, 1), 250 ms, no overshoot, within 1 percent by 0.64; cur-punchy-kick, cubic-bezier(0.2, 1, 0.25, 1.15), 350 ms, about 5 percent overshoot, loose band only. Say instead: 'a fast start with a decisive impact' not 'punchy copy'; 'the curve replayed as a repeating demo' not 'a for-loop'; 'three custom cubic-bezier curves with stated control points and measured overshoot and settle' not 'CSS ease'; 'a fast start that decelerates into a decisive landing' not 'linear motion'; 'a small overshoot, a few percent past the target, then a clean stop' not 'an elastic bounce'; 'the last frames sit still at the rest value' not 'an overshoot that keeps wobbling'; 'one overshoot on the first arrival, then a held rest' not 'a rebound on every loop'; 'a loop that stops and plays once on press' not 'autoplay with no stop'. Open: the prompt gives no control points, so the curves are proposed choices; sticky and punchy are defined here as observable motion, not established terms.

ak-loop-rebound.instead: one overshoot on the first arrival, then a held rest

ak-loop-autoplay.instead: a loop that stops under reduced motion and plays once on press

ak-punchy-copy.excluded_sense: punchy copy or a punchy audio mix
ak-punchy-copy.instead: a fast start with a decisive impact, described as motion

ak-loops-code.excluded_sense: a for-loop in code or a looping video file
ak-loops-code.instead: the curve replayed as a repeating demo

ak-ease-default.instead: Three custom cubic-bezier curves with stated control points and measured overshoot and settle, not a named preset.

ak-linear.instead: A fast start that decelerates into a decisive landing, with visible impact.

ak-overshoot-no-settle.instead: One brief overshoot, then a stop: the last frames sit still at the rest value.

ak-floaty-ease-in-out.instead: A steep start and a quick landing, about 200 to 400 ms for small UI.

ak-loop-jump-back.instead: Play the move, hold at rest for a visible beat, then reset; or ping-pong with a hold at each end.

ak-noise-intensifiers.instead: Name what the motion does instead: the peak speed, the overshoot and the moment it stops.

ak-sticky-css.excluded_sense: CSS position: sticky, or a sticky note or adhesive
ak-sticky-css.instead: motion that settles and holds without drift

ak-overshoot-large.instead: Small overshoot, 0 to 2 percent (proposed range); a 2 to 5 percent kick needs the loose settle band.

k-start-leaves-fast.text: Does the first window carry most of the distance, so the start reads as a response to the input rather than a drift?

test.spec: share of distance covered in the first 350 ms of a 1200 ms run; the sourced example covers 90 percent, so read reaches_50pct_at_x against the run length

k-stop-option-bands.text: Does the curve reach its settle band early enough that the last visible movement is short, judged under either band option?

test.spec: options per curves.options.cu-stop-check-options: A, within_1pct_from_x at or below 0.65; B, within_5pct_from_x at or below 0.35. A long crawl after the stop fails either option

k-no-drift.text: After the landing, does anything still move at a visible speed, such as a slow crawl over the last few pixels?

test.spec: change in the element's position per frame after the settle band is reached, at 60 fps; a tail that moves a pixel or more per frame reads as drift (illustrative threshold)

k-overshoot-small-single.text: Does the curve pass its target at most once, by a few percent, and then return to rest?

test.spec: passes above 1.0 after the first arrival (one at most) and overshoot_pct; the proposed curves measure 0, about 1.25, about 1 and about 5 percent

k-no-cartoon-bounce.text: Does the overshoot stay under about ten percent, where a back curve starts to read as a cartoon bounce?

test.spec: overshoot_pct of the curve; the back exemplar measures about 9.8 percent in this build and reads as bouncy

k-three-distinct.text: Do the three curves differ visibly in overshoot and settle time, so the loops show three feels rather than one curve three times?

test.spec: pairwise differences in overshoot_pct and within_1pct_from_x across the three curves; each pair differs on at least one of the two

k-ease-out-enter.text: Does an entering element leave fast and decelerate, rather than begin slowly?

test.spec: initial slope of y over x at x=0 (peak_speed_initial) against the average slope of 1; an entering curve sits above 1

k-duration-small-ui.text: Does the duration sit in the short band for small UI motion, with leaving shorter than entering?

test.spec: duration_ms against the sourced bands: small desktop 150 to 200 ms, entering about 225 ms, leaving about 195 ms, large about 375 ms

k-frames-spread.text: Are painted frames spread along the whole path, so no stretch of the motion reads as a jump?

test.spec: step the loop frame by frame and mark each tenth of the path; each tenth should hold at least one painted frame (illustrative granularity)

k-rest-hold-options.text: Does the rest hold last long enough to read the rest state, with the hold kept in the loop rather than the curve?

test.spec: hold_ms in the loop period against move_ms; options per curves.options.cu-rest-hold: 400 to 500 ms at each end of a ping-pong, or 1000 to 1500 ms between reset-and-hold cycles

k-loop-shows-curve.text: Does the loop show the arrival and the rest state on screen, with the curve's shape visible beside the moving element?

test.spec: one full loop, paused at the landing and again at rest; the arrival and the held rest are both in frame, and any curve-graph marker moves with the element

q-curve-settle-band.text: Which settle band defines sticky for these curves: 1 percent or 5 percent?
q-curve-settle-band.impact: Decides whether a visible kick is allowed (5 percent) or the stop must read as decisive (1 percent)
q-curve-settle-band.resolve: ask the user, or take the default

q-control-points.text: The prompt gives no control points; the three curves are the build's proposed choices, not the user's.
q-control-points.default: Use the three labeled proposed curves, with their measured overshoot and settle.
q-control-points.impact: every curve value and every loop
q-control-points.resolve: ask the user for control points, or keep the proposed set

q-sticky-punchy.text: Sticky and punchy have no fixed meaning; here they are defined as observable motion behavior.
q-sticky-punchy.default: Sticky means settles and holds without drift; punchy means a fast start and a decisive impact.
q-sticky-punchy.resolve: ask the user which observable behavior they mean

q-set-pick.text: Which three curves form the set?
q-set-pick.default: Set A: punchy leave cubic-bezier(0.2, 1.2, 0.2, 1) at 250 ms; punchy-sticky cubic-bezier(0.15, 1, 0.2, 1.04) at 300 ms; sticky settle cubic-bezier(0.18, 0.98, 0.3, 1) at 250 ms (strict 1 percent band)
q-set-pick.resolve: the user picks a set; the options group holds the alternatives

q-one-curve-both.text: Must each curve carry both sticky and punchy, or may the pair split across the set?
q-one-curve-both.default: split across the set, as Set A does; one curve carrying both stays an option
q-one-curve-both.impact: which curve is judged on which feel

q-settle-band.text: Is sticky judged by the 1 percent or the 5 percent settle band?
q-settle-band.default: 1 percent strict band (cu-settle-bands option A); 5 percent is option B
q-settle-band.impact: whether the punchy leave passes sticky

q-loop-return.text: Are the reset jump and the ping-pong return leg judged for drift?
q-loop-return.default: judged by measure and by eye; the reset jump is a deliberate cut, not drift

q-js-form.text: Which JS form: a WAAPI easing string or a sampled timing function?
q-js-form.default: WAAPI easing string with the cubic-bezier value; a sampled function is new code, not in the dump

q-repair.text: What to tune when a check fails?
q-repair.default: adjust overshoot first, then the stop band, then the duration; no repair map is sourced

request._about: The user's own words, verbatim from the prompt.

p-curves.anchor: a set of three custom bezier curves
p-curves.text: The deliverable is a set of three custom bezier curves.

p-feel.text: Each curve is described as feeling sticky and punchy.

p-loops.text: The curves are to be presented as loops.

motion_principles._about: Discipline primer for motion design, UI animation, and easing and timing theory, as they apply to a short motion with a fast start and a settle. Researched facts cite fetched sources; derived lines are inferred.

mp-cubic-model.text: A cubic-bezier curve is set by two control points, P1 and P2. The x values must stay in 0 to 1; the y values are progress and are not limited to 0 to 1.
behaviors: A y value above 1 lets the value pass the end state and come back
An x value outside 0 to 1 makes the declaration invalid
A P1 near the origin with a high y gives the fastest early speed
mp-cubic-model.principle: The x axis is the time axis and is fixed; the y axis is progress, and that is where overshoot and punch come from.
signals: y value above 1 in a cubic-bezier call
x value above 1 in a cubic-bezier call

tokens.y_range: not limited by the cited definitions

mp-overshoot-settle.text: A y value above 1 carries the value past its end state and brings it back; that single pass is the overshoot. The settle is the return to rest with nothing still moving after the landing.
behaviors: The value passes the target once and comes back
The overshoot is the visible impact at the end of the motion
mp-overshoot-settle.principle: Follow-through is the part still moving after the main action; the settle is where it stops.
signals: value crosses the end state once
motion stops with no slow creep at the last frame

mp-ease-out-enter-ease-in-leave.term: ease-out for entering, ease-in for leaving
mp-ease-out-enter-ease-in-leave.text: Ease-out starts abruptly and slows toward the end. Ease-in starts slowly, speeds up, and then stops abruptly.
behaviors: An element that enters uses ease-out so it lands softly
An element that leaves uses ease-in so it exits fast
Ease-in ends abruptly, so it suits exits and is a poor choice for a settle
mp-ease-out-enter-ease-in-leave.principle: Arriving things decelerate into place; leaving things accelerate away.
signals: fast first frames then a slow approach on entry
slow first frames then a hard stop on exit

mp-punch-fast-start.term: punchy as a fast start and a decisive impact
mp-punch-fast-start.text: Punchy means the curve leaves quickly and lands with a clear, small impact. The fast early speed is what the eye reads as response.
behaviors: Peak speed comes early when P1 sits near the start
A fast start with a short duration reads as a crisp hit
A small overshoot adds impact without a wobble
mp-punch-fast-start.principle: Speed at the start is what makes a motion feel responsive; the end decides whether it feels decisive.
signals: most distance covered in the first third of the duration
one small pass past the target

mp-common-mistakes.text: Typical mistakes: an overshoot too large, a tail that drifts after landing, and an ease keyword picked by habit.
behaviors: A y well above 1 reads as a wobble, not a snap
A long low-speed tail after the end reads as drift
The ease keyword is a default curve, so it looks unchosen
mp-common-mistakes.principle: A curve should look chosen, and the element should be at rest when the motion ends.
signals: value crosses the target by a visible margin
motion still creeping on the last frames

mp-ui-dos-donts.term: small UI motion: dos and don'ts
mp-ui-dos-donts.text: Keep small UI motion short, give each element one clear curve, and let the motion end when the visible change ends.
properties: reduced motion keeps the position change only
behaviors: Press feedback stays short and small
Drawers and toggles share one curve rather than bouncing individually
Under reduced motion the overshoot is removed and the position change remains
mp-ui-dos-donts.principle: Small UI motion should be felt more than watched.

mp-anticipation-slow-in-out.term: anticipation and slow in, slow out
mp-anticipation-slow-in-out.text: Anticipation is a small move the other way before the main action. Slow in and slow out puts more frames near the start and end of an action. Both come from the twelve basic principles of animation.
mp-anticipation-slow-in-out.principle: A preparation makes the action read as real, and the slow ends make the motion read as weight.
signals: small move opposite to the main move before it starts
frames bunch up at the start and end

motion_vocabulary._about: Words people use for how a motion arrives and rests. Preset names are sourced; the match to sticky and punchy is the build's reading.

sp-vocab.term: snappy, bouncy, pop and crisp motion words
sp-vocab.text: Spring-preset words name how a motion arrives and rests: snappy settles fast with a tactile finish, bouncy overshoots and rebounds, pop bursts in with a small kick.
behaviors: A snappy motion settles quickly with a slight tactile finish
A bouncy motion overshoots and rebounds before it rests
A pop motion bursts into place and kicks once at the end
A crisp motion is tight and controlled and locks in cleanly
sp-vocab.principle: Preset names describe the arrival and the rest, not the curve numbers, so pair each word with a measured overshoot.
signals: one visible rebound for bouncy
fast arrival then a short settle for snappy
sp-vocab._note: decisive stop and clean settle are the build's associations, not sourced terms.

sticky_punchy._about: What sticky and punchy mean as observable motion behavior in this build: readings of the prompt's words, not established terms. Collected facts (researched) sit beside the derived feel facets (inferred, checked against this build's measured curves); options name neighboring feels.

options._about: options, not requirements: nearest known relatives of the feels. Use them to name a neighbor, not as definitions of sticky or punchy.

feel-relatives.text: Four nearby feels: snappy settles quickly, bouncy overshoots and rebounds, tactile adds a small finish, and crisp is tight and locks in.
behaviors: Snappy is close to sticky with a faster arrival
Bouncy is close to punchy only when the rebound is visible
Tactile and crisp describe the last few frames more than the whole run
feel-relatives.principle: Relatives mark a neighborhood; sticky and punchy are still defined by the stop and the start.

sp-readings.term: sticky and punchy as motion behavior
sp-readings.text: Sticky reads as a motion that lands and holds with no drift; punchy reads as a fast leave and a decisive impact. These are readings of the prompt's words, not established terms.
behaviors: Drift after landing breaks the sticky reading
A fast departure from the start reads punchy; an even pace reads calm
A short overshoot before the hold can carry the punch without drifting
sp-readings.principle: Each word names a stage: the start carries punchy, the rest carries sticky.
signals: no visible movement after the first settle
peak speed early in the run

sp-long-tail.text: A fast main move that ends in a long, slow crawl over the last few pixels.
behaviors: Most of the distance lands early, so the eye reads the stop as already done
A long crawl after landing reads as drift unless the crawl is nearly invisible
sp-long-tail.principle: A stop feels decisive when the last visible movement is short, not when the total duration is short.
signals: most distance covered in the first third of the duration
final pixels still moving long after the main move

sp-fast-leave.text: The element covers most of its distance almost at once, so the first frames carry the motion.
behaviors: A steep start makes the motion read as a punch rather than a drift
A steep start with a short duration reads as too fast at first and as unsettled, so the start needs a matching settle
sp-fast-leave.principle: A fast leave is only half of a punchy feel; the settle has to match it or the start reads as wrong.
signals: large share of the distance in the first third of the duration
first frames spaced far apart

sp-teleport-check.text: Trace the frames the element paints; a stretch with no painted frames reads as a jump, even when the curve looks smooth.
behaviors: Frames bunched at one end of the path mean the element jumps across the empty side
Tuning the handles until frames are spread across the whole path removes the jump
sp-teleport-check.principle: Check where frames land, not only how the curve reads on a graph; a curve can look right and still skip.
signals: ghost frames bunched at one end
empty stretch with only the starting frame
even spacing across the path after tuning

feel-sticky.text: The motion arrives, stops decisively, and holds with nothing moving after the landing.
behaviors: Most of the distance lands early, so the stop reads as already done
A crawl left after the visible stop reads as drift and breaks the sticky reading
A short overshoot followed straight into a hold keeps the stop sticky
feel-sticky.principle: Sticky is about the end of the motion: the last visible movement is short and clean.
signals: no visible movement after the first settle
within 1 percent of target well before the duration ends
at most one short return

feel-punchy.text: The motion leaves fast, carries most of its distance in the first frames, and lands with a visible impact.
behaviors: A steep start reads as a response to the input rather than a drift
A small visible overshoot or kick at the landing gives the impact its shape
Peak speed early in the run is what makes the motion read as punchy
feel-punchy.principle: Punchy is the start: the first window carries the motion and the eye reads it as response.
signals: large share of the distance in the first window
peak speed in the first window
first painted frames spaced far apart

feel-pairing.text: One curve that starts with a punch and ends with a clean hold: the start carries punchy, the rest carries sticky.
behaviors: A steep start followed by a long crawl reads punchy and then drifting, so the tail has to be short
A steep start that paints no frames for the first half reads as a jump, so frame spacing needs checking as well as the curve
A short overshoot between the punch and the hold can carry both feels without a visible rebound
feel-pairing.principle: The two words name two stages of one motion, so a curve that has both is tuned at both ends.
signals: peak speed early
last visible movement short
one return at most

feel-tension.text: The productive tension is between a decisive stop that holds and a lively motion that overshoots and rebounds.

behaviors: The stop lands with no rebound, so the hold reads as firm
The target is passed and returned to, so the motion reads as alive

feel-tension.principle: Sticky sits on the decisive pole and punchy's start is shared by both; the impact tips toward lively as the overshoot grows.
signals: zero or one overshoot (decisive side)
two or more returns after the target (lively side)

feel-non-feels.text: Four failure modes sit near the target feel: a floaty drift, a wobbly rebound, a jump across unpainted frames, and a shaking or cartoonish bounce.
behaviors: A long crawl over the last few pixels reads as floaty or dragging
An overshoot of about 10 percent with one return reads as a bounce, and several returns read as wobbly
Frames bunched at one end read as a jump, even when the graph looks smooth
feel-non-feels.principle: Each non-feel comes from one property pushed too far: tail length, overshoot count, or frame spacing.
signals: within 1 percent of target only near the end of the duration (floaty)
more than one return after the target (wobbly)
an empty stretch of painted frames (jump)

feel-measures.text: Share of distance in the first window, overshoot percent and settle time, read on a normalized curve, separate the feels. Expo settles earliest with no return; back reaches 90 percent sooner but settles last.
properties: share of distance in first window
behaviors: A higher share of distance in the first window reads as a stronger start, which is the punchy measure
Overshoot percent separates crisp (none) from bouncy (around 10 percent for the back curve, 9.8 measured)
Settle time, the normalized x where progress stays within 1 percent of target, separates sticky from floaty
feel-measures.principle: Each feel has one headline number; check a curve against the number, not against how it looks.
signals: overshoot_pct
within_1pct_by_x
distance_pct_first_window

feel-element-fit.text: Press feedback fits punchy with no return; a toggle fits sticky with a short settle; a drawer fits sticky over a longer, even run; a card fits a small lively overshoot at most.
properties: card: decisive or one small return
behaviors: A press has to land before the finger lifts, so its punch stays short
A toggle changes state, so its stop is the moment the user reads
A drawer covers a large distance, so a long even run reads better than a steep start
feel-element-fit.principle: Match the duration to the distance and put the stop where the user needs to read the new state.
signals: press duration in the small-UI range
toggle stop visible at the state change
drawer distance covered across most of the run

curves._about: Three proposed cubic-bezier curves for sticky and punchy, with measured properties from this build's stdlib arithmetic (parametric sampling, bisection for x). Options, not requirements: the prompt gives no control points. Published curves are shown as references.

options._about: options, not requirements: three proposed curves; control points and measured properties are this build's computation, not a source

cur-punchy-leave.text: Leaves at high speed, passes its target by about 1.25 percent once, and is within 1 percent of rest by 0.64 of its run. A small kick, then a quiet stop.
behaviors: Half the distance is covered by 9 percent of the duration, so the start reads as a hit
The single pass beyond target peaks at 53 percent of duration, then returns inside the 1 percent band before the last third
Under the 1 percent band a fast leave carries only a faint kick; a visible 5 percent kick needs the 5 percent band (cur-punchy-kick)
cur-punchy-leave.principle: Under a 1 percent settle, a single cubic-bezier with a fast leave can carry only about a percent of overshoot before the return runs past the sticky line.
signals: one pass beyond the target, about 1 percent
within 1 percent before 0.65 of the run

tokens.replaces: cubic-bezier(0.2, 1, 0.25, 1.15) at 350 ms: within 1 percent only at 0.949, so it failed k-stop-decisive; that curve now lives on as cur-punchy-kick

overshoot_ceiling_1pct_band.note: best found by random sampling, not exhaustive

cur-punchy-sticky.text: Leaves fast, shows a faint overshoot under 1 percent, and is within 1 percent of rest by 0.46 of the run. Passes both the punch check and the stop check at the 1 percent band.
behaviors: Ninety percent of the distance is covered by 27 percent of the duration, so the start still reads as a hit
Within 1 percent by 0.46 of the run, so the stop reads well before the last third
The 5-to-1 percent tail is about 12 percent of the duration, short enough to read as a stop rather than a crawl
cur-punchy-sticky.principle: A faint overshoot that lands early is the one shape here that keeps both the punch and the stop under the strict band.
signals: overshoot under 1.5 percent
landing before the last third

cur-sticky-settle.text: Leaves fast, lands with no overshoot, and is within 1 percent of rest by 0.64 of the run. It carries no landing kick; the kick comes from cur-punchy-leave or cur-punchy-sticky.
properties: rest reached before two thirds of the run
behaviors: The curve stays at or below its target, so no drift shows after landing
Within 1 percent by 0.64 of the run, at the sticky line of 0.65 in feel-measures (illustrative)
The 5-to-1 percent tail is about 21 percent of the duration, so the stop is decisive but not instant
cur-sticky-settle.principle: Sticky without overshoot comes from landing early with nothing passing the target, so the hold reads as already done.
signals: no point above 1
rest reached before two thirds of the duration

tokens.earlier_value: cubic-bezier(0.16, 0.9, 0.22, 1) at 250 ms: within 1 percent at 0.684, over the 0.65 line

cur-punchy-kick.text: The visible kick: leaves fast, passes its target by about 5 percent once, then returns. Reads as sticky only under the 5 percent settle band; it gives up the 1 percent half.
behaviors: Half the distance is covered by 11 percent of the duration, so the start reads as a hit
The overshoot peaks at 61 percent of duration, so the pass-through is visible before the return
Within 1 percent only at 0.95, so about 18 ms still moves toward rest at 350 ms; use it under the 5 percent band or not at all
cur-punchy-kick.principle: A visible kick needs room to overshoot and return, so this curve trades the strict stop for a clear impact.
signals: one pass beyond the target of 3 to 6 percent
within 5 percent before a third of the run
never_implies: a long drift under the 1 percent band

cu-settle-bands.term: settle band options: 1 percent or 5 percent
cu-settle-bands.text: Two settle bands, offered as options. The 1 percent band is the strict stop; the 5 percent band is looser and allows a visible kick. Pick one per job; the dump does not impose either.
behaviors: Under the 1 percent band the three proposed curves stop at 0.46 to 0.65 of the run, and the kick at 0.95
Under the 5 percent band the kick stops at 0.31 of the run, so it reads sticky while its last 4 percent still crawls to rest
Choose the 1 percent band when the stop must read as decisive; choose the 5 percent band when a visible kick matters more
cu-settle-bands.principle: The band decides which half is given up: the strict band forbids a visible kick, the loose band allows it.
signals: stop point read at each band
crawl length after the stop

cu-stop-check-options.text: Stop check, as options. A (strict): within 1 percent of rest by about 0.65 of the run. B (loose): within 5 percent by about 0.35 of the run. A fast leave with a long crawl after its stop fails either option.
behaviors: A fast leave that keeps creeping for the last third reads as drift under either option
Option A is the default for sticky in this build; option B lets a visible kick through
cu-stop-check-options.principle: The stop is judged by where the curve reaches its band, not by how fast it starts.
signals: within_1pct_from_x at or below 0.65
within_5pct_from_x at or below 0.35

tokens.note: replaces the single rule in checks.k-stop-decisive once synthesis rewrites the spine

cu-rest-hold.text: How long the rest state holds is an option: about 0.4 to 0.5 s at each end of a ping-pong, or about 1 to 1.5 s between reset-and-hold cycles. The hold lives in the loop, not in the cubic-bezier.
behaviors: A hold shorter than about 0.4 s cuts the landing off before the eye reads the rest state
A hold of 1 to 1.5 s lets the stop read as held, and matches the proposed 1.44 s in loops
Write the hold as animation-delay or a final keyframe hold, never inside cubic-bezier()
cu-rest-hold.principle: The stop is judged in the hold, so the hold gets the time and the curve only supplies the landing.
signals: hold longer than the move
landing visible before the reset

cu-overshoot-bound.text: Overshoot bound, as proposed ranges: 0 to 2 percent is small and fits the strict band; 2 to 5 percent is the kick range and needs the loose band; above 5 percent is large and reads as a bounce.
properties: back-curve reference at 9.8 percent sits in large
behaviors: Under the strict band the largest measured overshoot is about 1.5 percent, so the small range is the reachable one
A kick above 5 percent passes its target by more than a small wobble and needs a long return that reads as drift
cu-overshoot-bound.principle: Overshoot is the punch dial, and the settle band caps how far it can turn before the return reads as drift.
signals: overshoot_pct in each range
passes above 1.0 after first arrival

cu-naming.text: Write control points to two decimals, trimmed (0.2, 1.2, 1). Name tokens by role then curve: --ease-punchy-leave, --ease-punchy-sticky, --ease-punchy-kick, --ease-sticky-settle; durations as --dur-punchy-leave and so on.
behaviors: All measured values here come from two-decimal control points, so the numbers hold when the same values are copied
Role-first names keep the punchy and sticky halves visible in the token list
JS constants mirror the tokens in camelCase: easePunchyLeave, easePunchyKick, easeStickySettle
cu-naming.principle: Short, exact values and names that say the role make the set easy to find and easy to check.
signals: cubic-bezier values with two decimals
--ease- prefix on each curve

durations._about: Typical durations for small UI motion. Ranges, not rules; scale with size and travel.

ui-durations.text: Small desktop transitions run 150 to 200 ms and mobile transitions typically 300 ms; elements entering take about 225 ms and leaving about 195 ms. The Material scale runs 50 to 1000 ms.
behaviors: Leaving elements run shorter than entering elements
Larger or full-screen motion runs longer, around 375 ms
ui-durations.principle: Duration scales with size and travel: short for small, close movement.
signals: entering longer than leaving
small element finished within 200 ms

sp-exemplar-back.text: Ease-out with a y value above 1 on the first control point, so the motion passes its target by about 10 percent and returns.
behaviors: The peak overshoot lands at about 57 percent of the duration
After the peak the motion returns and is within 1 percent of rest by about 91 percent of the duration
sp-exemplar-back.principle: Overshoot comes from a control point value above 1, so it is a single dial on an otherwise plain ease-out.
signals: one visible pass beyond the target
a single rebound
sp-exemplar-back._note: Source is a third-party gist titled Unusual CSS easings, not Penner's own page; Penner lineage is not confirmed by a fetched source.

sp-exemplar-expo.text: Ease-out that leaves at high speed and spends a long tail near the target, with no overshoot.
behaviors: Half the distance is covered in about a tenth of the duration
The last 10 percent of distance is covered after about a third of the duration
sp-exemplar-expo.principle: Front-loaded speed gives the leave its force, and the long tail is what reads as settle.
signals: fast first third
no rebound

sp-exemplar-m3.text: Material standard is one cubic bezier. The emphasized curve is not a single bezier in the M3 spec, per a third-party port's doc comment, so the port aliases emphasized to standard. Emphasized-decelerate is a separate curve with a sharper start.
behaviors: Emphasized-decelerate reaches half the distance in about 6 percent of the duration, faster than standard
sp-exemplar-m3.principle: Material's curves are decelerating ease-outs without overshoot; they are the calm reference for a sticky settle.
signals: no overshoot
fast start then long settle
sp-exemplar-m3._note: Official m3.material.io values were not readable (the fetch returned the title only); the numbers come from a third-party port.

sp-bezier-range.text: x1 and x2 must sit in 0 to 1 so the curve stays a function of time. y1 and y2 are free: values above 1 overshoot the target and return, and values below 0 pull back before moving forward.
behaviors: A y value above 1 sends the value past its end state before it returns
A y value below 0 makes the motion start by moving backward
In spring terms, bounce 0 gives no overshoot and bounce above 0 gives one; above about 0.4 is too exaggerated for UI
sp-bezier-range.principle: Time must run forward; only the progress axis may exceed its bounds.
signals: value passes its end state
value moves the wrong way at the start
sp-bezier-range._note: No exact bezier equivalent of a spring was found in the fetched sources; stiffness and damping have no sourced numbers here.

cv-exaggerate-then-lengthen.text: Push a built-in ease-out to an extreme curve, then raise the duration until the settle reads as natural.
behaviors: An extreme curve at 500ms looks too fast at first and does not settle naturally
The same extreme curve at 1200ms glides to a stop smoothly, because most of the time is spent on nearly invisible motion
cv-exaggerate-then-lengthen.principle: A long duration with a steep curve spends most of its time on motion too small to see, so the animation feels short.
signals: handle pulled far from its default position
duration well above 500ms

cu-overshoot.text: A cubic-bezier curve with a y value outside 0 to 1 overshoots once, then settles. That single overshoot is its ceiling.
behaviors: A y value above 1 makes the motion pass its target once before settling
A y value below 0 makes the motion pull back once before leaving
A cubic-bezier curve cannot produce a second rebound or a ringing settle
cu-overshoot.principle: One control point pushed past its range buys one overshoot; a second bounce needs a different kind of curve.
signals: one visible pass-through of the target
no second rebound
cu-overshoot.quote: cubic-bezier() can overshoot once, but it can't produce multiple bounces or oscillation.
cu-overshoot._note: The article gives no overshoot percentage and no peak time for the example curve. The x range is not stated on the page.

cu-linear-keyframes.text: linear() interpolates between a list of output values; values above 1 or below 0 overshoot, so one curve can bounce several times.
behaviors: Each listed value is a stop and the motion moves straight between neighboring stops
A stop above 1 pushes past the target, and the next stop below 1 pulls it back
Stops that repeat smaller overshoots in turn produce a bouncing settle that a single cubic-bezier cannot
cu-linear-keyframes.principle: The curve is a sampled path, so any shape you can list as values is available, including several rebounds.
signals: values above 1 followed by smaller values above and below 1
several rebounds before rest
cu-linear-keyframes.quote: linear(0, 1.2 60%, 1) puts the overshoot at 60% of the duration rather than evenly spaced.
cu-linear-keyframes._derived: Spec rule: unhinted stops between hinted stops are spaced evenly. In the example that puts 0.9 near 73% and 1.05 near 87%, so the curve peaks at 1.2 at 60%, dips to 0.9, rises to 1.05 and rests at 1. This is inferred from the stop list, not stated on the page.

cu-js-route.term: JS route to bounce and spring
cu-js-route.text: The article's old route for bounce and spring is a JavaScript animation library with a spring easing string. The page shows no Web Animations API or custom easing function.
behaviors: The JS route needs a library and a spring string; the CSS route needs only a transition value
cu-js-route.principle: Pick the CSS route when the motion is one property on one element; the library route stays for springs that must be retuned at runtime.
signals: easing string like spring(...)
animation library import
cu-js-route._gap: No Web Animations API example appears on this page; the JS equivalent for a custom easing function is not sourced here.

cu-support.text: linear() shipped in Chrome and Edge 113, Firefox 112 and Safari 17.2, and the page marks it widely available with roughly 87 percent of users covered.
behaviors: Older browsers ignore the linear() value and fall back to the property's default timing
cu-support.principle: Ship linear() without a fallback only where the 2023 baseline covers your audience.
signals: browser version below the listed minimums
cu-support.quote: This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions.

cur-how-written.term: writing and measuring a cubic-bezier curve
cur-how-written.text: Four numbers define the curve: x1 and x2 stay between 0 and 1, while y1 and y2 set overshoot. The curve runs from (0,0) to (1,1).
behaviors: The initial slope equals y1 divided by x1, so a small x1 with a larger y1 leaves faster
A y2 above 1 is what produces the overshoot; y1 above 1 also overshoots
Settle time depends on how close y2 sits to 1 after the peak
cur-how-written.principle: Read the handles as departure speed (x1, y1) and arrival shape (x2, y2): the start sets the punch, the end sets the stick.
signals: values written as cubic-bezier() in CSS
easing: 'cubic-bezier(...)' in Web Animations API

tokens.measure_method: sample x(t) and y(t) at 20001 points, bisect for t at each x, record peak y, initial slope, first crossing of 50 and 90 percent, and the last x outside 1 or 5 percent of rest

cur-reference-shelf.text: Published curves to compare against, not tier-1 picks: ease-out-back for one overshoot, ease-out-expo for a fast leave with no overshoot, Material emphasized-decelerate for a sharp start.
behaviors: ease-out-back overshoots about 9.8 percent, a larger pass than the punchy option here
ease-out-expo leaves fast and has no overshoot, which is close to the sticky option here
cur-reference-shelf.principle: A known shape gives the reader a fixed point, so a proposed curve can be judged as more or less punchy than something familiar.
signals: overshoot size named in percent
half-distance point named as a fraction of duration

cu-browser-js-form.term: browser and JS form of a curve
cu-browser-js-form.text: The same curve runs in CSS as a timing function and in the Web Animations API as an easing string. Several rebounds need linear() stops instead of cubic-bezier().
properties: WAAPI: easing string in the options object
linear(): a stop list for multi-point curves
behaviors: element.animate(keyframes, { duration: 250, easing: 'cubic-bezier(0.2, 1.2, 0.2, 1)' }) runs the punchy leave
A JS function is only needed when the curve must be sampled rather than timed, since the easing string covers the timed case
linear() can list several rebounds that one cubic-bezier cannot; Chrome 113, Firefox 112 and Safari 17.2 are the support floor (cu-support)
cu-browser-js-form.principle: Use the string form for one property on one element; reach for linear() only when the curve needs more than one pass.
signals: easing: 'cubic-bezier(' in an animate call
transition-timing-function set to cubic-bezier

cu-duration-band.term: duration against the small UI bands
cu-duration-band.text: The leave and sticky curves run 200 to 300 ms, between the 195 ms leave band and the 225 ms enter band. The kick runs 300 to 350 ms, above the small-desktop band of 150 to 200 ms.
behaviors: The leave curve at 350 ms would run well above the 195 ms leave band, so it is set at 250 ms with a 200 to 300 ms range
At 200 ms the punchy leave settles within 1 percent at about 129 ms, which is the lowest it can run and keep its settle
The kick sits outside the leave band on purpose, because its overshoot needs the time to return
cu-duration-band.principle: The band is a floor for small motion; each curve's own settle sets how short it may run.
signals: duration_ms inside each stated range
settle_ms at or under the duration

cur-tuning-dials.term: tuning dials for the revised set
cur-tuning-dials.text: Three dials set the feel: overshoot size, departure slope and duration. Overshoot buys punch only while the settle band can still be reached by about 0.65 of the run.
behaviors: A larger overshoot adds punch and also lengthens the return, so the strict band caps it near 1.5 percent
A steeper initial slope adds punch but gives the eye less time to read the start
A longer duration lets the kick read, while the stop is judged in the hold
cur-tuning-dials.principle: Punch and stick trade through the tail: the more the curve overshoots, the longer the return it has to hide.
signals: overshoot above 2 percent under the strict band
5-to-1 tail longer than a fifth of the duration

decision_points.question: How much overshoot
decision_points.tradeoff: Overshoot gives the punch; a longer return reads as drift under the strict band

decision_points.question: How fast to leave
decision_points.tradeoff: Steeper leave reads punchier but gives the eye less time to read the start

decision_points.question: Duration
decision_points.tradeoff: Longer lets the overshoot read; shorter keeps the stop crisp

ui_application._about: Merged into curves.durations; entry moved there.

loops._about: How each curve is shown as a repeating demo: loop structure, timing, reduced motion and a CSS sketch. Structure and timing are proposed choices, not sourced rules; the one sourced number is the 1200 ms, 90%-in-350 ms example from a curve tool article. Options, not requirements.

options._about: Which curve role fits each UI element, shown as a press, toggle, drawer or card. Options, not requirements; the curve names come from the curves section. The loop is a demo device; product UI runs the motion once per interaction.

opt-press.text: A short punchy curve with a small overshoot, under 200 ms, suits a press.
opt-press.why: Small desktop transitions sit at 150 to 200 ms in the Material duration scale (sourced).

opt-toggle.text: A sticky curve with no overshoot, 200 to 250 ms, suits a toggle so the thumb lands without a rebound.
opt-toggle.why: Toggles share one curve, so the landing reads as one settle.

opt-drawer.text: A sticky curve with no overshoot, about 300 to 375 ms, suits a drawer that travels a long way.
opt-drawer.why: Larger and full-screen motion runs about 375 ms in the sourced Material duration scale.

opt-card.text: A punchy curve with one small overshoot, about 225 ms for the enter, suits a card or popover that appears.
opt-card.why: Entering elements take about 225 ms in the sourced duration scale.

editor._about: What a cubic-bezier curve editor shows beside its motion, read from the cubic-bezier.com screenshot and fetched text. Visual facets come from the screenshot; text facets come from the scraped chunk.

cb-curve-graph.text: The curve is drawn as a graph with time across and progression up, with two handles on lines from the endpoints, beside a preview block with a duration slider and a GO! button.
properties: time on x, progression on y
two handles on lines from endpoints
behaviors: Each handle shows the pull on one end of the curve, so its position maps to the bend beside it
The motion plays only when GO! is pressed
signals: curve graph next to a GO! button
duration slider with a seconds readout

cb-named-baselines.text: A row of named presets (ease, linear, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out) shows each as a thumbnail, and clicking one compares it with the current curve.
behaviors: Presets serve as reference shapes that a custom curve is compared against
The compare action puts a named preset beside the current curve
cb-named-baselines.principle: A named preset gives a known reference shape, so a custom curve can be read against something familiar.
signals: row of five named thumbnails
current curve highlighted in the row

cb-value-readout.text: The current curve is shown as a cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) call in the header, with each number coloured by handle and a COPY menu beside it.
behaviors: The COPY menu suggests the readout is the exact string to paste into CSS
signals: cubic-bezier(.17,.67,.83,.67) header
coloured numbers
COPY dropdown

loop-compare.term: curve preview with duration and compare
loop-compare.text: A curve explorer shows the curve value, a duration control, and a preview; clicking a curve swaps it in for comparison with the current one.
behaviors: Duration is a separate control from the curve shape, so one curve reads differently at different durations
Comparing two curves side by side is the editor's way to judge a feel
loop-compare.principle: A curve judged alone lacks the time it runs in; show the duration with the curve.
signals: duration shown next to the curve
two curves compared on one preview

lp-structure.text: Reset-and-hold suits a settle: the motion runs once, holds at rest, then jumps back to the start. Ping-pong shows both directions but changes how the return feels.
behaviors: Reset-and-hold keeps the landing and the held rest state on screen, which is the part a sticky curve is judged on
Ping-pong with animation-direction alternate runs the curve backward in time on the return, so an ease-out returns as a slow start and fast arrival
A ping-pong return with its own curve needs an explicit keyframe, not the alternate flag
lp-structure.principle: The loop should show the part of the curve that matters: for a settle, that is the arrival and the hold.
signals: rest held on screen
return leg slower than the outbound leg
lp-structure._note: The alternate-direction behavior follows the CSS animation model (timing applied to directed progress); confirm in a browser before relying on it.

lp-period-hold.text: A one-way move of about 1.2 s covers 90 percent of its distance in the first 350 ms, so the readable part is the start; the held rest follows as a long settle.
behaviors: A longer move gives the eye time to read the settle, but a hold that is too short cuts the landing off before it reads
The hold should be long enough to read the rest state; around a second or more is the proposed floor
Ping-pong adds two holds, so its period is longer than reset-and-hold at the same move length
lp-period-hold.principle: Period is move plus hold; the hold is where the stop is judged, so it gets the time.
signals: hold longer than the move
landing visible before the reset

lp-shown-elements.term: what the loop shows: dot on track, curve graph, value readout
lp-shown-elements.text: The demo can show the moving element alone, or add the curve graph with a moving marker and a numeric readout beside it. The editor's own preview has no loop by default.
behaviors: A marker on the curve graph, moved with the same timing as the dot, shows the bend while the motion runs
A readout of the progress value shows where the curve passes 1.0, which is where an overshoot appears
cubic-bezier.com plays only when GO is pressed, so a loop has to be added deliberately
lp-shown-elements.principle: Showing the curve next to the motion lets a reader match the feel to the shape, which motion alone does not.
signals: graph and dot share one clock
readout above 1.0 on overshoot curves

lp-reduced-motion.term: reduced-motion fallback for a looping demo
lp-reduced-motion.text: Under reduced motion the loop stops and the demo shows the rest state, with a press-to-play-once control for anyone who wants the motion.
behaviors: Stopping the loop removes repeated motion, which is the main vestibular trigger for a demo
Play-once starts only from a user press, so nothing moves without a request
Removing overshoot in the fallback would hide the curve's character, so keep it only if the loop itself is dropped
lp-reduced-motion.principle: A reduced-motion reader still gets the curve's value and its end state; the moving part is what is removed.
signals: no animation running
press control present

decisions.decision: show the curve graph or the motion alone

options.fits_when: the reader needs to match the feel to the shape
the demo is for a feel check, not a teaching page
the rest state is what is judged
the reverse motion is part of the test, with its own return curve

lp-keyframes.term: CSS keyframes for the reset-and-hold loop
lp-keyframes.text: A single keyframe loop puts the curve on the first segment, a linear hold on the second, and resets at 100 percent. The curve is a custom property filled per curve from the curves section.
behaviors: Each keyframe's animation-timing-function applies to the segment that starts at that keyframe
The reset is the wrap from 100% to 0%, so the hold is a stop and not a fade
lp-keyframes.principle: Putting the curve on the outbound keyframe keeps the hold linear, so the stop belongs to the curve alone.
signals: keyframes with animation-timing-function per stop

lexicon._about: Associations for sticky and punchy motion, one entry per register. Seed material at tier 3 to 4; they widen the vocabulary and do not define the curves.

lx-technical.text: The technical words for a motion curve: timing function, control points, progress, overshoot and settle.

lx-perceptual.term: how the motion feels: sensory words
lx-perceptual.text: Touch and sound words people use for a motion that lands with a firm, clean feel.

lx-emotional.text: Emotional words for a motion that feels confident and alive without drifting into play.

lx-sticky-adjacent.text: Words for a motion that arrives and stays put, with nothing creeping after the landing.

lx-punchy-adjacent.text: Words for a motion that starts with force and hits its target with a small impact.

lx-domain-objects.text: The parts a curve loop or editor shows: handles, tracks, frames and readouts.

influences._about: Lineages behind named easing curves. Contributions only; nothing here is a style to copy.

inf-penner._note: No fetched source confirms this lineage; treat the naming as a common association.
contribution: back and expo as named families
curves people reach for by name
short, medium and long duration tiers
an emphasized curve for the main move
deceleration when entering and acceleration when leaving
spring motion set by duration and bounce rather than a fixed curve
interruptible motion that keeps its velocity
a bounce setting that trades overshoot against settle
a small pull-back before the main move
slow in and slow out for weight
draggable handles with a live preview
a frame-spacing check for teleport gaps
